newsitem.title: USA: U.S. blue chips end lower but broader market firm.
newsitem.headline: U.S. blue chips end lower but broader market firm.

text.p: U.S. blue chips closed lower on Thursday for the second straight session, shedding some of the gains posted earlier this week as investors mulled the Federal Reserve's decision to leave rates unchanged.
The Dow Jones industrial average unofficially closed down 33 at 7258.

Still, the broader market showed some strength, with slightly more issues advancing than declining on the New York Stock Exchange and a key index of small-capitalization stocks, the Russell 2000, closing in positive territory.
Weakness in the blue chips came on the heels of a 13-point Dow loss on Wednesday, as the index trimmed some of the gains of more than 100 points struck earlier this week.

"We're been giving back some of the gains from that euphoric spike-up. But with the wild volatility in the market, which is here to stay, we need to digest gains in order to lessen the volatility above 7000," said Scott Bleier, chief market strategist for Prime Charter Ltd.

The Dow losses came amid weakness in bonds, with the yield on the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond touching the key 7.00 percent threshold during the day. Late in the session, the long bond was off 11/32 to yield 6.99 percent.

Zigzagging in bonds after the release of minutes from the Fed's March board meeting lent stocks no clear direction, analysts said. The panel voted to move to a neutral policy, from a tightening bias, at the same time it raised rates.
"When negative comments were published from the minutes, bonds sold off. When positive comments came out, bonds came back," said Dick Stein, vice president at U.S. Clearing Corp.

In stocks, analysts said the Dow's decline masked some positive developments. Breadth was about even with a slightly positive bias, and small-cap and technology stocks fared better than the blue chips.

"Many technology companies easily make 50 percent or more of their revenues overseas, and they got killed earlier this year with the rise in interest rates and also because the dollar was so high," said Lary Aasheim, vice president at CoreStates Investment Advisers Inc.
With the Fed's decision to leave rates alone, recent weakness in the dollar and relatively cheap valuations, the Nasdaq could "absolutely" topple its record high, he said.
Gainers beat decliners on the NYSE, with 1,271 stocks gaining and 1,175 falling. On the Big Board, 156 stocks hit new highs while only 13 hit new lows.
Breadth was also positive on the Nasdaq, where 2,158 stocks rose and 2,003 fell. There were 143 fresh highs in stocks compared with 61 new lows.
Among individual issues, shares of Gateway 2000 Inc, a direct marketer of personal computers, and Brazil's Unibanco Group SA encountered heavy trading in their NYSE debuts.

Unibanco's American Depositary Receipts rose 5/8 to 34-3/8. Gateway -- the 31st company to move from the Nasdaq to the NYSE this year -- caused a stir by bringing a cow to the floor of the venerable exchange. The stock fell 3/4 to 68-1/2.
Mail Boxes Etc rose 3 to 22-5/8 after agreeing to be acquired by U.S. Office Products in a stock swap worth $276.9 million. U.S. Office Products lost 7/8 to 23-5/8.

Hartford Life Inc shares jumped 13 percent after the initial public offering of the eighth-largest U.S. life insurer. Hartford Life, a unit of Hartford Financial Services Group Inc, closed up 3-7/8 to 32-1/8.
The Nasdaq closed off 1.15 at 1372.60.
The S&P 500 fell 3.69 to 835.66.
About 430.1 million shares were traded on the NYSE.
((-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1881))
